metadata.title: Cultivating Green Futures: Helping students understand and progress towards green jobs

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD policy brief does not conduct a student-level statistical analysis with a defined analytic sample from PISA 2018; instead, it synthesises descriptive PISA results (e.g., shares of students agreeing with statements) and combines them with a scoping review of green guidance programmes. Because no microdata modelling is reported, there is no documented application of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for estimation. The brief cites PISA 2018 database tables for percentages and statistically significant differences, which in the OECD/PISA production process are typically computed using PISA’s complex survey design, but the brief itself does not specify weight variables. For any re-analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA sampling weights and plausible-value procedures for cognitive domains, and use replicate methods as recommended by the PISA technical documentation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because this document is a policy brief and scoping review that reports descriptive results and programme evidence rather than estimating achievement outcomes from PISA plausible values. The brief does not specify any missing-data strategy because it does not present an original student-level modelling workflow (e.g., no imputation/deletion procedure for an analytic dataset). As a result, PV and missing-data handling are not part of the methods reported in this document.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief draws on PISA 2018 descriptive results (e.g., OECD averages and country/economy shares) and on a scoping review of 87 green guidance programmes across 20 OECD countries. It does not define a student-level analytic sample with inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade band, task completion, or missingness rules) for an original empirical model.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD policy brief uses PISA 2018 as an evidence base to illustrate young people’s engagement with environmental issues and a gap between caring about climate change and perceived agency to contribute to solutions. It reports descriptive indicators such as the share of 15-year-olds expressing confidence in understanding climate change impacts (78% on average across OECD countries) and the smaller share who feel they can actively contribute (57%), alongside the finding that personal interest in environmental protection exceeds perceived agency in every country/economy. The brief also synthesises a scoping review of 87 green guidance programmes across primary to upper secondary education in 20 OECD countries, describing programme objectives and design features (e.g., career exploration, applied learning, employer/workplace experiences, and personalised guidance). Rather than estimating causal effects, it proposes a framework for “green guidance” grounded in broader OECD evidence on career readiness and employment outcomes. Limitations include the absence of an explicit student-level modelling design, no reported ML evaluation, and no documented PV/missing-data handling for an original analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy brief and scoping review rather than an empirical ML study with a defined analytic dataset, model training, and reported predictive metrics. Consequently, fields such as total_students, per-country student counts, and PV/missing-data handling for an original estimation workflow are not provided because the brief does not run a new student-level statistical model. The extraction therefore focuses on the evidence sources (PISA 2018 descriptive tables and the programme scoping review) and on the conceptual framework proposed for green guidance.
